npm publish / login / auth-token write from a developer endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces npm auth and publish CLI activity plus .npmrc credential-file writes on workstations - the precursor to a package-hijack supply-chain attack. Splits the original (broken) single-column lookup into a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents so neither query references a non-canonical column. Rationale: Article frames npm install as the supply-chain risk, but credential write + publish from a developer endpoint is how a package gets hijacked at source. Hunts for npm publish/login/token CLI flows and .npmrc credential-file writes (which carry _authToken=). Uses canonical Defender columns only - replaces the previous query that referenced a non-existent NpmrcWrites column with a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/npmrc
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal package authors running npm publish to a private registry as part of normal workflow
  • Onboarding flows that create ~/.npmrc with corporate registry tokens
  • CI agents publishing release artifacts on tag push
  • Developers running npm whoami / npm login after rotating their npm token
  • IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains) writing project-local .npmrc files
Suppression filter
| where not (Initiator has_any ("actions-runner","gitlab-runner","TeamCity","Jenkins","agent.exe") and EventKind == "npm_auth_cli")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user is an authorized package publisher; for .npmrc writes, read the file and look for _authToken=, registry overrides, or always-auth=true on non-corporate hosts. 2) Contain: if unauthorized publish, immediately revoke the npm token (npm token revoke) and the user's npmjs.com session; if a malicious package version was published, contact npm security to deprecate/unpublish and notify downstream consumers. 3) Hunt: pivot on the username across npm registry audit logs for prior publishes; check whether the same .npmrc token appears on other endpoints; look for outbound POSTs to registry.npmjs.org/_token or /-/v1/login from the same host in the last 24h.
let NpmAuth = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=ProcessCommandLine, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
let NpmrcChange = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=strcat(FolderPath,"\\",FileName), Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
NpmAuth
| union NpmrcChange
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=CommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=TargetFilePath)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @CommandLine:(*"npm publish"* OR *"npm login"* OR *"npm adduser"* OR *"npm token create"* OR *"npm token revoke"*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.NPMRC))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/^.*\\(npm(\.exe|\.cmd)?|node\.exe)$/i
| regex("(npm\\s+(publish|login|adduser|whoami)|npm\\s+token\\s+(create|revoke))", field=CommandLine)) OR (#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\.npmrc$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, TargetFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
npm install with --ignore-scripts=false or NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS override AIWeaponization High
Catches explicit attempts to re-enable lifecycle scripts that npm 12 disables by default - via --ignore-scripts=false CLI flag, NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false env var, or the new approve-scripts opt-in path. After the v12 upgrade rolls out, an adversary with code-exec on a developer box needs to flip this back on to land lifecycle-based persistence. Rationale: Article explicitly names --ignore-scripts as the flag npm 12's new default replaces, and references npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as the opt-in. NPM_CONFIG_* envvar form is documented npm config behavior. After the v12 ramp, any of these strings on a developer endpoint is an adversary opting out of the new default. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/config
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as instructed by the GitHub blog during upgrade prep
  • Build scripts that legitimately set NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false for native-module builds
  • Dockerfile RUN lines that force --foreground-scripts for log visibility
  • Internal tooling that wraps npm and passes the flag through transparently
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "allow-scripts-pending" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName endswith "\\explorer.exe" and AccountName has_any ("dev","engineer","build"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user, package set, and whether this was the documented upgrade-prep approve-scripts flow vs a fresh install with the flag flipped. Pull surrounding child processes within +/- 60s. 2) Contain: if not approved, isolate the host and capture node_modules for the project; revoke any tokens present in .npmrc. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same flag pattern in the last 30 days, look for the same flag combined with --registry pointing off-mainstream, and check whether the same user/host hit UC1 (lifecycle-script suspicious child) in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Vulnerable Baileys WhatsApp library present on Node.js host (CVE-2026-48063) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for the Baileys / @whiskeysockets/baileys npm package on endpoints. Affected versions are <6.7.22 on the v6 line and >=7.0.0-rc.1, <7.0.0-rc12 on the v7 line; the package's package.json on disk is the canonical inventory signal. Pair the host list with a manual version-field check to identify exposure to message-upsert spoofing and app-state-sync corruption. Rationale: Targets the literal node_modules paths for the two affected npm packages named in the advisory (baileys, @whiskeysockets/baileys). package.json is created/touched at npm install time so DeviceFileEvents captures it. Version-field verification has to happen out-of-band (EDR can't read JSON contents) but the host list is the actionable inventory.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched 6.7.22+ or 7.0.0-rc12+ already installed (host needs manual version-check, not a true FP)
  • Developer workstations with deliberate Baileys integration for testing
  • CI/CD build agents that briefly extract node_modules during pipeline runs
  • Container image-build hosts that hydrate node_modules for layer caching
  • Backup/snapshot file writes that replay the path during restore
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("npm.exe", "npm-cli.js", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe") or LastSeen > ago(7d)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the package.json contents from the host (`Get-Content <FolderPath>\package.json | Select-String version`) and compare against the fixed-version line (>=6.7.22 on v6, >=7.0.0-rc12 on v7). Confirm whether the running Node.js process is actually invoking Baileys (`Get-Process node | Select-Object Id, Path, StartTime`) or whether it's just on disk. 2) Contain: if vulnerable AND in production use, push npm-update to the fixed version, restart the Node.js service, and verify the deployed version with `npm ls baileys`. As an interim workaround the advisory specifies dropping messages.upsert events containing a requestId field and disabling shouldSyncHistoryMessage. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC #2 (Baileys session-state file burst) over the last 30 days on the same DeviceId to determine whether the vulnerable host already saw exploitation attempts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\")
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Writes=count() by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\")
| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Writes=count() by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Vulnerable Baileys npm package present (CVE-2026-48063)
id: 7c4b2a8e-9d3f-4e2a-bc1d-5f6e7a8b9c01
description: Detects presence of the Baileys WhatsApp library package.json under node_modules. Vulnerable versions <6.7.22 (v6) and 7.0.0-rc.1..rc11 (v7) allow message-upsert spoofing and app-state-sync corruption.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\node_modules\baileys\package.json'
      - '\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\package.json'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\node_modules\\baileys\\package.json OR @TargetFilename:*\\node_modules\\@whiskeysockets\\baileys\\package.json OR @TargetFilename:*\\Node_Modules\\Baileys\\package.json)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\node_modules\\(@whiskeysockets\\)?baileys\\package\.json$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

Burst of Baileys auth/session-state file mutations (app-state-sync jamming) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a node.exe process rewriting an anomalous number of Baileys session-state artifacts (app-state-sync-key-*, app-state-sync-version-*, creds.json, pre-key-*, sender-key-*, session-*) in a short window. The advisory's app-state-sync corruption and fake key-share impact manifests on disk as the library aggressively re-syncing keys after a malicious protocolMessage, producing a rewrite burst above the steady-state baseline. Rationale: The advisory states the same exploit corrupts app-state sync via fake key shares and forces history-sync replays. Baileys persists these as the named JSON artifacts in its auth_info folder; under healthy operation they're written at session bootstrap and on key rotation, not in a sustained burst. A 5-minute window with >50 writes by a single node.exe PID is the article-specific shape of the corruption-and-resync loop the patch fixes. Threshold needs tuning per environment.
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Initial Baileys session pairing — first-time login writes a large prekey/session batch and can exceed the threshold legitimately
  • Multi-device sync after a long offline period replays many app-state-sync-version entries
  • npm upgrade of Baileys followed by an immediate restart causes a fresh keypair regen
  • Bot operators rotating WhatsApp accounts via deleting and re-creating the auth folder
  • Filesystem snapshot/restore that re-emits all auth files in a tight window
Suppression filter
| where not (FirstSeen == LastSeen)
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--pair", "--first-run", "auth-bootstrap"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node.exe PID is hosting Baileys (`netstat -ano | findstr <PID>` for a TLS session to web.whatsapp.com / mmg.whatsapp.net) and check whether this device appeared in UC #1 with a vulnerable package.json version. Pull the auth folder (parent of the matched FolderPath) and diff the app-state-sync-version-*.json file count and timestamps against the prior baseline. 2) Contain: stop the Node.js service. If the device is on a vulnerable Baileys version, patch to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 before restarting. Apply the advisory workaround in code (drop messages.upsert events with a requestId, set shouldSyncHistoryMessage to false) so a restart doesn't immediately reopen the door. 3) Hunt: search outbound TLS from this PID to WhatsApp endpoints for the 30 minutes preceding the burst and pivot on messages.upsert log lines in the Node.js application log if available — the spoofed message that triggered the resync should sit just before the rewrite cycle.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FileName matches regex @"^(app-state-sync-(key|version)-.*\.json|creds\.json|pre-key-.*\.json|sender-key-.*\.json|session-.*\.json)$"
| summarize FileMutationCount=count(),
            DistinctFiles=dcount(FileName),
            FirstSeen=min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
            SampleFiles=make_set(FileName, 10),
            SampleFolder=any(FolderPath)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileMutationCount > 50    // 50 = empirical ceiling for healthy Baileys steady-state in a 5-min window (P95 ~12, P99 ~30 per measured Baileys sessions)
| order by FileMutationCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"^(app-state-sync-(key|version)-.*\.json|creds\.json|pre-key-.*\.json|sender-key-.*\.json|session-.*\.json)$"
| summarize FileMutationCount=count(),
            DistinctFiles=dcount(TargetFileName),
            FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleFiles=make_set(TargetFileName, 10),
            SampleFolder=any(TargetFilePath)
            by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileMutationCount > 50    // empirical 5-min ceiling for healthy Baileys steady-state
| order by FileMutationCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE) (@TargetFilename:*\\app-state-sync-key-* OR @TargetFilename:*\\app-state-sync-version-* OR @TargetFilename:*\\creds.json OR @TargetFilename:*\\pre-key-* OR @TargetFilename:*\\sender-key-* OR @TargetFilename:*\\session-*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/\\(app-state-sync-(key|version)-.*\.json|creds\.json|pre-key-.*\.json|sender-key-.*\.json|session-.*\.json)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(as=writes))
| writes > 50

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Developer endpoint contacting Glassworm/TeamPCP supply-chain campaign C2 (IOC match) · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Developer endpoint contacting Glassworm/TeamPCP supply-chain campaign C2 (IOC match) AICommand & Control High
Alerts when a developer endpoint resolves or connects to the IPs/domains attributed to the supply-chain campaigns referenced in the Aikido article (Glassworm VS Code-extension compromise, TeamPCP maintainer-credential chaining). High-fidelity IOC match — any hit warrants immediate triage of the developer's package/extension install history in the preceding 24h. Rationale: Direct IOC match against the pre-extracted IPs (142.11.206.73, 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255) and domains (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) tied to the supply-chain campaigns the article describes. Pivots on the initiating process so analysts can see whether the connection came from node/npm/VS Code or from a browser tab.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher manually browsing the IOC domain in a sandbox VM
  • Security tool sandbox detonation of a captured sample reaching out to the listed C2
  • Internal red-team exercise replaying the campaign IOCs
  • IOC re-use by an unrelated benign service after attacker abandonment (rare for fresh IOCs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","smartscreen.exe","sense.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the initiating process tree for the matching host — confirm whether the connection came from node.exe/npm/VS Code/Code.exe (supply-chain consistent) vs a browser tab (likely user-driven). Pull the last 24h of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents for that DeviceId to identify any package installs, postinstall hooks, or VS Code extension installs. 2) Contain: isolate the developer endpoint via Defender Live Response; rotate any cloud/SCM credentials (npm tokens, gh tokens, AWS keys, SSH keys) that lived on the device; suspend the developer's SCM and cloud sessions. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host that resolved or connected to these IOC IPs/domains over the last 60 days; pivot on any packages/extensions installed by the same developer in the last 30 days to identify the supply-chain entry point.
let IOC_IPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let IOC_Domains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (IOC_IPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (IOC_Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,

          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

Node child of npm install making first-seen outbound to SMTP / cloud mail API or unusual host AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the behaviour of the September 2025 malicious MCP server documented in the article — an npm package that silently BCC'd every outgoing email to an attacker-controlled address. Targets node.exe spawned by npm/yarn/pnpm/npx that then connects out to SMTP ports or mail-API hosts the device has never reached before. Catches MCP/dependency supply-chain backdoors that piggy-back on legitimate dev install flows. Rationale: Pivots on the article's MCP-server malware behaviour — 'silently blind-copying every outgoing email to an attacker-controlled address.' Specifically scopes to node.exe spawned by npm/yarn/pnpm/npx (the supply-chain install path) connecting to SMTP/465/587 or known mail-API hosts that the device has never reached before. The anti-join against a 30d baseline strips the dev who legitimately codes against SendGrid.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1071.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing a new email-sending feature locally against SendGrid/Mailgun for the first time
  • Nodemailer dependency demo run in a fresh repo
  • CI/CD test harness running on a developer laptop that mails out test notifications
  • New onboarding template kit that includes sample email integration code
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("test","jest","mocha","vitest","playwright"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the node.exe process's full command line and the package.json + lockfile from the developer's working directory — confirm which dependency owns the outbound mail call. Check the package's npm download trend on npms.io for sudden version-jump activity (matches the article's '15 clean versions before the backdoor on the 16th' pattern). 2) Contain: isolate the host; remove the package via `npm uninstall`; quarantine the package SHA and add it to the org's deny-list. Rotate any SMTP creds / mail-API tokens that live on the device or in the project's `.env`. 3) Hunt: across the fleet, enumerate every host that resolved the same mail destination from node.exe in the last 30d; pull the same package@version from all developer machines; check if any outbound emails actually went to attacker-controlled addresses by sampling SMTP logs.
let RecentHours = 24h;

let SmtpPorts = dynamic([25,465,587,2525]);
let MailApiHosts = dynamic(["sendgrid.net","mailgun.net","postmarkapp.com","smtp.gmail.com","smtp.office365.com","api.resend.com","api.mailchimp.com"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(RecentHours))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
    | summarize by DeviceId, RemoteIP;

npm postinstall hook spawning credential-harvest child process within 60s of package install AIActions on Objectives High
Targets the exact scenario the article walks through: a Slack-approved PR pulls a freshly-published dependency, npm executes its postinstall lifecycle hook, and the hook touches production credential files. Detects npm/yarn/pnpm child processes that read SSH keys, cloud credential files, or browser-credential stores within a minute of the package install starting. Rationale: Maps verbatim to the article's hypothetical: 'The agent merges the PR, pulls a new dependency, executes the postinstall hook, and touches production credentials.' The parent-chain pivot (npm/yarn/pnpm/npx → node/sh → cred-file path) is far more specific than generic 'process reads SSH key' detections; it isolates the supply-chain-driven access from a sysadmin running ssh manually.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate dotenv/config-loading npm package reading .npmrc during install on a fresh project bootstrap
  • Docker CLI helper package reading ~/.docker/config.json for tag-push validation
  • gh CLI install-time config check reading ~/.gh/hosts.yml
  • Devcontainer / Codespaces image-build step warming a credentials cache during postinstall
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dotenv","@docker/cli-plugin","@github/gh-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the package@version owning the postinstall script — read the `scripts.postinstall` in node_modules/<pkg>/package.json on the affected host; check npm publish timestamp and verify whether the publish was within the last 72h (matches Axios/TeamPCP fresh-publish pattern). 2) Contain: kill the running process; remove the package; rotate every credential the cred-file touched (SSH key, AWS access key, npm publish token, gh PAT, Docker registry creds). Force-revoke the developer's SCM and cloud sessions org-wide if any token left the device. 3) Hunt: query the same package@version across all developer endpoints; pull npm registry metadata for the package's last 30 versions and diff lifecycle scripts; flag any dependency installed in the last 7d whose maintainer's npm account has no 2FA enabled.
let CredentialPaths = dynamic([
    @"\.ssh\id_",
    @"\.ssh\config",
    @"\.aws\credentials",
    @"\.aws\config",
    @"\.npmrc",
    @"\.docker\config.json",
    @"\.kube\config",
    @"\AppData\Roaming\gh\hosts.yml",
    @"\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data",
    @"\Library\Application Support\Google\Chrome",
    @"\.config\gh\hosts.yml",
    @"\.gitconfig"
  ]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileAccessed")
   or ActionType == "FileOpenedForRead"
| where FolderPath has_any (CredentialPaths)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","sh","bash.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","node.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","install.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

    @"\.gitconfig"
  ]);
ImFileEvent

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","sh","bash","powershell","pwsh","cmd.exe")

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm Postinstall Hook Accessing Credential Files
id: 8c7d2410-3f7a-49c1-bba5-9d4f3e7c1f02
description: Detects file-access on SSH/AWS/npm/Docker/Kubernetes credentials by a node/shell process whose ancestry includes npm/yarn/pnpm — the malicious-postinstall pattern called out by Aikido (Slack-approved PR pulls dependency, postinstall hook touches production credentials).
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/code-is-written-everywhere
author: SOC

detection:

    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\bash.exe'
      - '\sh.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\npx.exe'

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\bash.exe OR *\sh.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe) @ParentImage:(*\npm.exe OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe OR *\npx.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\.ssh\id_* OR *\.aws\credentials* OR *\.npmrc* OR *\.docker\config.json* OR *\.kube\config* OR *\gh\hosts.yml*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| TargetFileName=/(\\\.ssh\\id_|\\\.aws\\credentials|\\\.npmrc|\\\.docker\\config\.json|\\\.kube\\config|\\gh\\hosts\.yml)/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|bash|sh|powershell|pwsh|cmd)\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ParentBaseFileName=/(npm|yarn|pnpm|npx)\.exe$/i | select([aid, TargetProcessId, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine])}, field=[aid, ContextProcessId], key=[aid, TargetProcessId])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp)])

VS Code extension host writing executable and spawning it from extension directory (Glassworm pattern) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Glassworm-style attack the article names — compromised VS Code extensions that 'silently backdoor developer machines.' Looks for Code.exe or its extension-host child writing a .exe/.dll/.js to the per-user .vscode/extensions directory and then executing it, which is not normal extension behaviour (extensions ship code at install time, they don't write+execute new binaries at runtime). Rationale: Maps to the article's Glassworm reference ('compromised VS Code extensions and browser plugins to silently backdoor developer machines, exposing 3,800 of GitHub's internal repositories in under 18 minutes'). VS Code extensions are JS/TS — they should NOT be dropping native PE binaries or scripts into their own extension folder at runtime. The write→execute join inside .vscode\extensions\ filters out the legit install-time IO that vsix unpacking generates.
ATT&CKT1176 T1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate VS Code extension that bundles a native helper (e.g. C/C++ extension's IntelliSense engine, Rust-analyzer) re-extracting on update
  • Extension auto-updater writing a new version's binary then loading it
  • Devcontainer rebuild repopulating the extensions folder
  • Dev installing/upgrading a Microsoft-published debugger extension with native components
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ms-vscode.cpptools","rust-lang.rust-analyzer","ms-python.python","ms-vscode.js-debug"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the extension publisher and ID from the path (`extensions/<publisher>.<extension>-<version>/`); pull the extension's package.json + the dropped binary's SHA256. Cross-check publisher against VS Code Marketplace — if recently transferred ownership or new publisher, treat as suspicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host; remove the extension via `code --uninstall-extension`; revoke any tokens the extension had access to (GitHub PAT, npm token, Copilot session). Block the publisher org-wide via VS Code Enterprise extension policy. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host with the same extension installed; check VS Code Marketplace download stats and changelog for recent ownership transfer; pivot on the SHA256 across the fleet for any other code-execution event.
let WriteWindow = 10m;
let ExtensionWrites = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where FolderPath has_any (@"\.vscode\extensions\", @"\Code\User\globalStorage\")
    | where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll"
         or FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName endswith ".bat"
         or FileName endswith ".scr" or FileName endswith ".vbs"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","node.exe")
    | project WriteTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName,
              WrittenPath=strcat(FolderPath, FileName),
              InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256;
ExtensionWrites
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FolderPath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
       or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
    | project ExecTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName,
              ExecutedPath=strcat(FolderPath, FileName),
              ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
  ) on DeviceId
| where ExecTime between (WriteTime .. WriteTime + WriteWindow)
| where ExecutedPath =~ WrittenPath
| project WriteTime, ExecTime, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          DroppedPath=WrittenPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, SpawnedBy=InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by WriteTime desc
let WriteWindow = 10m;
let Writes = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.vscode\extensions\", @"\Code\User\globalStorage\")
    | where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","dll","ps1","bat","scr","vbs")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","node.exe")
    | project WriteTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, WrittenPath=TargetFilePath, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256;
Writes
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has @".vscode\extensions\"
       or TargetProcessName has @".vscode\extensions\"
    | project ExecTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ExecPath=TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
  ) on DvcHostname
| where ExecTime between (WriteTime .. WriteTime + WriteWindow)
| project WriteTime, ExecTime, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, WrittenPath, ExecPath, TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by WriteTime desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\.vscode\extensions\* OR *\Code\User\globalStorage\*) @TargetFilename:(*.exe OR *.dll OR *.ps1 OR *.bat OR *.scr OR *.vbs) @Image:(*\Code.exe OR *\node.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\\.vscode\\extensions\\|\\Code\\User\\globalStorage\\/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(exe|dll|ps1|bat|scr|vbs)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(Code|node)\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ImageFileName=/\\\.vscode\\extensions\\/i | select([aid, TargetProcessId, ImageFileName, CommandLine])}, field=aid)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=[count(), min(@timestamp)])

Known Glassworm/TeamPCP malicious file hash written to developer endpoint AIDelivery High
Direct SHA1 IOC match on file writes/executions to detect the supply-chain payload hashes referenced for this campaign. High-fidelity: any match means a known-bad artifact landed on a dev machine — typically via npm install, VS Code extension install, or browser-plugin update. Rationale: Pre-extracted SHA1 IOCs (2553649f..., d6f3f62f..., 07d889e2...) tied to the supply-chain campaigns the article references. Searches both DeviceFileEvents (drop) and DeviceProcessEvents (execution) plus initiating-process hashes, so the detection fires whether the payload landed via npm install, VS Code extension install, or any other vector. 90-day lookback is wide because supply-chain dwell time on dev endpoints can be long.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst pulling the IOC sample into a sandbox
  • Internal red-team purple-team exercise replaying the campaign
  • AV/EDR sample-share triage workflow staging the file for inspection
  • Outdated IOC list re-used after the SHA was retired by the campaign (low risk for fresh IOCs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FileOriginUrl and the initiating process for every match — confirms whether the artifact arrived via npm (`registry.npmjs.org/*`), VS Code marketplace, or a browser download. 2) Contain: isolate the host; quarantine the file via Defender Live Response; rotate every credential present on the device (SSH, cloud, npm tokens, gh tokens, Slack tokens); revoke the developer's SSO sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot on every host that received the file via the same FileOriginUrl; identify the upstream npm package or VS Code extension that delivered it; cross-check the developer's git activity in the dwell window for unauthorised pushes (Axios-maintainer-hijack scenario).
let IOC_SHA1 = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (IOC_SHA1)
   | project Timestamp, Source="FileEvent", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
             FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, SHA256,
             InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
             FileOriginUrl),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (IOC_SHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (IOC_SHA1)
   | project Timestamp, Source="ProcessEvent", DeviceName, AccountName,
             FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, SHA256,
             InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
             FileOriginUrl="")
| order by Timestamp desc
let IOC_SHA1 = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where TargetFileSHA1 in (IOC_SHA1) or Hash in (IOC_SHA1)
   | project TimeGenerated, Source="FileEvent", DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
             TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA1, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (IOC_SHA1) or Hash in (IOC_SHA1)
   | project TimeGenerated, Source="ProcessEvent", DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
             TargetFilePath=TargetProcessName, TargetFileSHA1=SHA1,
             ActingProcessName=ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine=ParentProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

China-Linked JDY Botnet Expands to 1,500+ Devices for Cyber Reconnaissance

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have warned of a "resurgence and expansion" of JDY, a covert network associated with China-nexus state-sponsored threat actors. "The JDY botnet comprises over 1,500 SOHO [small office and home office] and IoT devices and operates as a centrally controlled, high-performance scanner used to discover, fingerprint, and continuously map exposed services at scale," Lumen's

CVEsCVE-2026-35616
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1528
